claims.text: As-received Q235 low-carbon steel typically has a fine-grained microstructure.
At 700–900 °C, a high density of grain boundaries in fine-grained Q235 accelerates diffusion of oxygen and aggressive salt species.
Accelerated transport along grain boundaries causes rapid and non-uniform oxide formation.
Rapid, non-uniform oxide formation increases oxide cracking, spallation, and corrosion damage.
A coarser grain structure restricts diffusion of oxygen and aggressive salt species through Q235.
Restricted diffusion in coarse-grained Q235 promotes a more uniform and adherent protective oxide film.
Higher-temperature annealing promotes grain growth and can generate a coarser-grained condition than lower-temperature annealing.
Annealing treatments near 700 °C and 900 °C can produce predominantly fine- and coarse-grained Q235 variants while otherwise preserving relevant material variables.
The 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl environment is a molten aggressive salt over the proposed 700–900 °C test range.
Grain boundaries act as fast-diffusion channels for oxygen and salt species during high-temperature corrosion.
Coarse-grained Q235 will exhibit lower mass loss than fine-grained Q235 during high-temperature molten-salt exposure.
Coarse-grained Q235 will exhibit fewer oxide cracks and less spallation than fine-grained Q235 during high-temperature molten-salt exposure.
Coarse-grained Q235 will form a more uniform oxide scale than fine-grained Q235 during high-temperature molten-salt exposure.
At room temperature, slow diffusion makes corrosion differences between fine- and coarse-grained Q235 minimal.
The proposed grain-size mechanism applies predominantly at 700–900 °C and is negligible under ambient or low-temperature conditions.
Precipitates, residual stresses, and minor compositional variations may alter the quantitative relationship between grain size and corrosion rate.
